title: Wharves, Jetties, Quays and Marine Terminals
analyses: Global and local structural strength analysis
Berthing energy and vessel impact analysis
Mooring force and bollard load analysis
Wave, current, wind and tidal loading analysis
Deck, beam and slab loading analysis
Ultimate and serviceability limit state analysis
Accidental damage and progressive collapse analysis

models.text: The suite should implement static force and moment equilibrium, Euler–Bernoulli beam theory, Timoshenko beam theory, Kirchhoff–Love and Mindlin–Reissner plate theories, reinforced concrete sectional analysis, elastic and nonlinear frame analysis, matrix stiffness methods, classical elasticity, plasticity, column buckling, plate buckling, ultimate limit state and serviceability limit state formulations. Reinforced concrete modelling should incorporate cracked-section analysis, moment–curvature relationships, concrete compression stress–strain models, steel reinforcement plasticity, shear resistance models and time-dependent creep and shrinkage relationships.

The suite should employ vessel kinetic energy formulations, effective berthing mass models, eccentricity and hydrodynamic mass coefficients, nonlinear fender force–deflection models, energy absorption relationships, nonlinear impact dynamics, contact-impact mechanics, momentum transfer and vessel approach trajectory models. Mooring forces should be evaluated using line tension equilibrium, catenary theory, nonlinear line elasticity, environmental vessel force models and dynamic mooring analysis.

The suite should include Rankine and Coulomb earth pressure theories, Terzaghi and Meyerhof bearing-capacity models, Winkler foundations, lateral pile resistance curves, axial pile shaft and toe resistance models, pile-group interaction, elastic settlement, consolidation, Mohr–Coulomb plasticity, Modified Cam-Clay, liquefaction triggering correlations and nonlinear soil–structure interaction.

Wave loading should use Airy, Stokes and stream-function wave theories, Morison's equation, diffraction theory, wind and tidal current models, spectral wave models, vessel-induced wave loading and wave impact formulations. Local scour calculations should incorporate Shields sediment mobility, bed shear stress models, empirical pile-scour correlations, sediment continuity equations, bed-load transport models and suspended sediment transport equations.

Applicable methods include modal analysis, response spectrum methods, time-history analysis, S–N fatigue curves, rainflow cycle counting, Palmgren–Miner damage, chloride diffusion models, Fick's diffusion laws, reinforcement corrosion initiation and propagation, section-loss calculations, crack-growth models and time-dependent structural reliability.

The suite should integrate vessel berthing simulations with nonlinear fender and structural dynamics, CFD wave-load simulations with structural finite elements, geotechnical finite-element analysis with pile-supported deck models, corrosion deterioration with reliability-based life prediction, and stochastic vessel traffic modelling with probabilistic berthing load assessment.

inputs.text: Wharf length, jetty width, quay height, deck elevation, slab thickness, beam dimensions, pile spacing, pile rake angles, retaining-wall geometry and berth arrangement.

Fender type, dimensions, energy absorption curves, reaction-force curves, fender spacing and allowable deflection.
Bollard capacities, mooring-hook ratings, line stiffness, line strength, line arrangements and vessel fairlead positions.
Container loads, cargo storage loads, truck axle loads, crane wheel loads, rail-mounted gantry loads, personnel loads and loading/unloading machinery.
Water levels, tides, waves, currents, storm surge, wind speeds, water depth and vessel-induced hydrodynamic conditions.
Borehole data, soil strength, foundation stiffness, pile penetration depths, bearing resistance and lateral soil resistance.
Ground-motion spectra, acceleration histories, soil liquefaction susceptibility and lateral spreading estimates.
Reinforcement arrangement, pile caps, pile heads, deck connections, expansion joints and support restraints.
Corrosion rates, chloride exposure, crack records, concrete deterioration, pile section loss and previous repair history.
Berthing limits, allowable deck deflection, settlement tolerance, load combinations, fatigue life and design vessel requirements.

subtitle: Port and marine terminal structural strength, vessel berthing, mooring, foundation capacity and operational serviceability.
ic: The initial conditions shall establish the constructed geometry of the wharf, jetty, quay wall or marine terminal, including deck slabs, girders, piles, pile caps, retaining structures, fenders, bollards and expansion joints. The initial structural state shall include permanent dead loads, installed equipment and the prevailing structural stresses.

The initial geotechnical conditions shall specify soil layering, earth pressure conditions, groundwater levels, pore-water pressure, pile embedment and foundation settlement. Where quay walls retain backfill, the initial lateral earth pressure state and backfill compaction conditions shall be established.

For berthing analysis, the approaching vessel shall initially have a specified position, heading, transverse or longitudinal approach velocity, displacement and contact configuration. Fender deformation and initial contact forces shall be defined according to whether the simulation starts before first contact or after contact has begun.

For mooring analysis, initial vessel position, mooring line lengths, line pretension, water level and environmental forces shall establish the initial equilibrium. Existing infrastructure shall include the initial corrosion, concrete cracking, pile deterioration, settlement and inspection findings relevant to reassessment.
bc: Foundation boundary conditions shall represent pile–soil resistance, retaining-wall earth pressure, soil stiffness, bearing support and the effects of changing groundwater levels. Structural connections between slabs, beams, pile caps and piles shall transmit the intended forces and moments.

Marine boundaries shall specify water-level variation, tidal action, wave pressure, current loading, hydrostatic pressure and uplift. Deck boundaries shall prescribe cargo storage, crane wheel loads, vehicle axle loads, equipment loads and personnel loading.

For berthing, fender boundaries shall use the actual nonlinear force-deflection characteristics, vessel contact geometry and impact direction. Mooring boundaries shall prescribe forces transferred through bollards, hooks, mooring lines and their supporting structures.

For seismic conditions, appropriate ground-motion histories and soil deformation shall be imposed. Scour analysis shall use near-bed velocities, sediment properties and erosion boundary conditions. Structural deterioration analysis shall prescribe the environmental exposure and corrosion or material-degradation conditions over the intended service period.

calibration: Calibration should use port structural monitoring, pile load tests, geotechnical site investigations, berth impact measurements, fender compression tests and mooring load records.

Fender force-deflection and energy absorption properties should be calibrated using certified laboratory tests and representative operating-temperature and compression-rate conditions. Vessel berthing parameters should be informed by measured approach velocities, berthing angles, vessel displacement and impact locations.
Pile–soil interaction models should be calibrated against axial and lateral pile load tests, measured pile-head movements and observed quay settlement.

Structural stiffness should be calibrated using measured deck deflections, pile-cap movements, modal testing and strain-gauge data. Concrete stiffness, cracking behaviour and reinforcement response should be informed by appropriate material and structural experiments.
Mooring force models should use line tension records, bollard load measurements and documented vessel loading conditions.
Scour and sediment transport models should be calibrated against bathymetric surveys, sediment measurements and observed changes around piles and marine foundations.
Structural deterioration parameters should be calibrated using corrosion measurements, chloride penetration tests, concrete condition surveys, crack mapping and maintenance records.
verification: Verification should include analytical and numerical benchmarks for deck slabs, beams, pile caps, piles, retaining walls and foundation systems.
Finite-element mesh convergence should be demonstrated for reinforced concrete members, steel connections, pile-supported decks and regions of concentrated berthing loads.

Berthing energy calculations should be checked against independently calculated reference cases, while fender force-deflection interpolation and energy integration should be verified using certified test curves.
Mooring reactions, bollard loading and vessel environmental forces should undergo equilibrium and force-resolution checks.
Pile and foundation calculations should be verified through lateral and axial pile benchmarks, soil-structure interaction tests and bearing-capacity reference solutions.
Seismic analyses should undergo response-spectrum consistency checks, time-step convergence and soil liquefaction implementation testing.
Scour calculations should be verified through sediment conservation checks and spatial-temporal convergence studies.
Progressive collapse and deterioration analyses should be tested using controlled structural degradation and member-removal benchmarks.
validation: Structural response should be validated against monitored wharves and jetties under known cargo, crane and vessel loading.
Berthing impact predictions should be compared against recorded berthing velocities, fender compressions, impact forces and measured structural movements.
Mooring force predictions should be evaluated against instrumented bollards and mooring lines under representative vessel and weather conditions.
Foundation response should be validated using full-scale pile load tests, settlement monitoring and independent geotechnical field observations.
Scour predictions should be assessed against repeat seabed surveys around operating marine structures.
Seismic and liquefaction models should be evaluated using independent physical-model experiments or well-documented earthquake case histories.
Structural deterioration and remaining-life predictions should be compared with successive inspection campaigns, observed corrosion progression, concrete damage and repair histories.

geometry.text: Piled wharves, quay walls, jetties, berthing structures, reinforced concrete decks, steel platforms, retaining walls, pile caps, fender supports, bollard foundations, container terminals and marine loading facilities.

geometry.cat: Conventional and universal CAD geometry formats
geometry.text: STEP (.step, .stp), IGES (.iges, .igs), Parasolid (.x_t, .x_b), ACIS (.sat, .sab), IFC (.ifc), DXF (.dxf) and supported DWG (.dwg) should be accepted for structural members, concrete decks, foundations, retaining walls, pile caps, fender assemblies and marine terminal equipment supports.

geometry.cat: Civil infrastructure and BIM geometry formats
geometry.text: IFC 4.3 infrastructure representations, LandXML (.xml), CityGML (.gml, .xml), InfraGML, GML, GeoPackage (.gpkg) and compatible civil alignment and surface models should be supported where their contents include suitable geometry. IFC 4.3 is particularly relevant because its scope includes infrastructure such as waterways and port facilities.
SDNF, CIS/2, Nastran BDF/NAS, Abaqus INP, ANSYS CDB, Gmsh MSH, MED, UNV, VTK/VTU and Exodus should be accepted for imported beam, shell, solid, foundation and soil–structure interaction models.

LAS/LAZ, E57, XYZ, PLY, OBJ, STL, GeoTIFF, ESRI ASCII Grid, LandXML surface data and bathymetric point clouds should be supported for as-built wharves, quay-wall deformation surveys, seabed profiling and existing marine infrastructure reconstruction.
